Web design in Marshall, TX has a deadline built into it, and it arrives every holiday season. That is when Wonderland of Lights turns the downtown square into the busiest place in Harrison County and visitors start searching for somewhere to eat, shop and stay. Dominion Web Design Pro builds sites for Marshall businesses that want to be found when that happens, and all the months in between: every page written by hand by Maurice Johnson, with a free demo before you spend anything.

A festival that started as a newspaper column

In 1987 Marshall was in a hard spot, with unemployment near twenty percent. George S. Smith, then editor of the Marshall News Messenger, walked across downtown, pictured the Harrison County Courthouse strung with lights, and wrote about it. A Marshall native living in France answered with a check for $25,000, and the town built the rest. Today the courthouse is wrapped in lights every holiday season, and the festival has grown to include an ice rink and a historic carousel.

The story matters to a business owner because it shows how Marshall works: the town decided to bring people downtown, and it did. Every year since, visitors who have never been here walk the square with phones in their hands. The shops, restaurants and inns they can find online get their business. The ones they cannot find do not.

A Marshall website timeline that beats the rush

Search engines need time to find and trust a new site. Working back from the lights, this is the schedule that gives a Marshall business a real chance at holiday searches.

  1. Spring: ask for the demoGive your business name and what you sell. Look at the demo on your phone and decide whether to go ahead.

Who is searching for Marshall businesses

Marshall had 23,392 residents at the 2020 census, but its customer base is much wider than its population. The town was founded in 1841 and named for Chief Justice John Marshall, and it has been a crossroads ever since. The first telegraph office in Texas opened here in 1854. The Texas and Pacific Railway later made Marshall a railroad town, and Amtrak's Texas Eagle still stops at the depot. Marshall also sits on Interstate 20, between Shreveport to the east and Longview and Dallas to the west.

Put together, that gives a Marshall shop an unusually mixed crowd: people who live here, festival visitors, interstate travelers, day-trippers from Louisiana and business travelers in town for a few nights. They have one thing in common. None of them will find you by driving past.

Behind the downtown, Harrison County has a working economy of its own: manufacturing, oil and gas, and the businesses that serve them along the I-20 corridor. Contractors, mechanics, welders and supply companies sell to those operations, and their customers check a website before they call. A plain page per service, with the towns you cover, does that job well.

What a first-time visitor needs from your page

Picture a couple from Shreveport parked near the courthouse on a December evening. They have twenty minutes before the carousel line gets long, and they want dinner. They will open two or three sites, and they will leave any of them that makes them work. Here is what keeps them on yours.

  • Open or closed, today. Hours at the top of the page, with holiday changes posted as soon as you know them.
  • How far from the square. A sentence like "two blocks north of the courthouse" beats a map pin a stranger has to zoom into.
  • What it costs, roughly. A menu, a price range or a few example prices, so they know you fit what they planned to spend.
  • A way to call in one tap. Big enough for a cold thumb, at the top of every page.
  • Real photos. Your dining room, your shelves, your work. Stock pictures make visitors wonder what you are hiding.

None of that is fancy, and that is the point. The same page also works for the regular who drives in from Hallsville on a Tuesday in March, which is the customer who pays the bills the other ten months of the year.

Free help in Marshall

The UT Tyler-Longview Small Business Development Center keeps a Marshall office, which moved to Synergy Park in 2023, and gives free advising to businesses in Harrison County and five neighboring counties. The Greater Marshall Chamber of Commerce on South Bolivar Street is the place for introductions, events and referrals around the square. We have no arrangement with either of them. They are simply worth a call, and plenty of owners never make it.

Common questions

When should a Marshall business build a website for the Wonderland of Lights season?

In spring or early summer. A new site needs time to be found and indexed before it can show up in searches, so a site launched in November mostly misses the season it was built for. Aim to be live, with holiday hours ready to post, by the end of summer.

Who does web design in Marshall, Texas?

Dominion Web Design Pro is one option: Maurice Johnson, working from Big Sandy in Upshur County, writes and builds every page himself. You see a free demo of your Marshall site before you decide to buy anything.

My Marshall business makes most of its money in November and December. Is a website worth it?

That is one of the strongest reasons to have one. A seasonal business has a few weeks to reach people who have never heard of it, and search is the only channel that works that fast. The site has to be ready before the season starts, not during it.

How much does a website cost for a business in Harrison County?

$497, $997 or $1,997, one time, depending on the package. Hosting, maintenance and updates are $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent. The pricing page lists what each package includes.

Can my website reach customers coming over from Shreveport?

It can be written for them. A page that explains what you offer to day-trippers, with directions from I-20 and your hours, gives Google and those visitors something to find. The Pro package's 10 city pages can also cover towns like Hallsville, Waskom, Jefferson and Longview.
